extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (intro to proofs/discrete math)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and solution-style rubric for writing correct elementary-mathematics proofs: handling quantifiers, case analyses, set manipulations, relations, functions, uniqueness/existence, and induction. Includes common mistakes and example patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of quantifier introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce variables in the order required by the logical form of the statement; do not define an earlier variable in terms of a later arbitrary variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original guidance: “This outline makes it clear that y should be introduced into the proof after x. Therefore, x cannot be defined in terms of y, because y will not yet have been introduced into the proof when x is being defined.” Anti-pattern: defining x in terms of y before introducing y (disguised mistake when 'Let y be arbitrary' is omitted). Example: given ∀x ∃y φ(x,y), first 'Let x be arbitrary' then define y possibly depending on x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce an arbitrary element to prove universal statements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a universally quantified statement, begin by letting an arbitrary element be chosen, prove the desired property for that element, then conclude the universal statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern repeated: 'Let y be arbitrary. Then ... Since y was arbitrary, ∀y ...' Use this to prove statements like ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)) ⇒ ∀x P(x) by letting an arbitrary y and extracting P(y). Always end by stating that because the element was arbitrary you have the universal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential instantiation / selecting witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When given an existential premise or when proving existence, choose a witness (instantiate the existential) and work with that element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Since x ∈ UF, we can choose some A ∈ F such that x ∈ A.' Use this pattern to access properties of the witness. When proving ∃x, construct an explicit x (see constructive witness rubric) or use existential instantiation from hypotheses. When proving uniqueness, combine with the uniqueness pattern (assume two witnesses and show equality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove conjunctions under universals by extracting components
rubrics_metrics.description: From a universal conjunction ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)) deduce ∀x P(x) and ∀x Q(x) by letting an arbitrary element and taking each conjunct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example text: '(—) Suppose ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)). Let y be arbitrary. Then since ∀x(P(x) ∧ Q(x)), P(y) ∧ Q(y), and so in particular P(y). Since y was arbitrary, this shows that ∀x P(x).' Mirror reasoning proves ∀x Q(x). Use this two-direction structure when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set equality via mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets equal, prove each is a subset of the other by letting an arbitrary element of one side and showing it belongs to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: 'Let x be arbitrary and suppose x ∈ LHS. Then (case analysis if needed) ... therefore x ∈ RHS. Since x was arbitrary, LHS ⊆ RHS. Now prove RHS ⊆ LHS similarly.' Many worked examples: P(A∩B) = P(A) ∩ P(B), U(F∪G) = UF ∪ UG, etc. Emphasize arbitrary element and both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statement naturally splits by cases (e.g., sign, membership in a union), break the proof into exhaustive, mutually-exclusive cases and treat each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: absolute-value inequalities: handle x−4>0 and x−4<0; union/set membership: consider x∈A or x∈B. Warning: 'The cases are not exhaustive' is a common mistake. State cases explicitly and verify they cover all possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired conclusion and derive a contradiction with given hypotheses or previously proven facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used e.g. in showing disjointness: 'Suppose UF and NG are not disjoint... leads to contradiction.' Also suggested for one direction of biconditionals in some hints: use existential instantiation and contradiction. When using contradiction, clearly state the assumption and locate the contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive existence (give an explicit witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving an existential statement, provide an explicit formula or construction for a witness (e.g., y = x/(x^2+1)), and then verify it satisfies the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Section 3.6: 'Let y = x/(x^2 + 1). ... To see that y is unique, suppose ...' Concrete construction simplifies verification and uniqueness checks. If you can solve the defining equation for the witness, present that algebraic solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness proofs (existence + uniqueness argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove uniqueness of an object with a property, first show existence, then assume two such objects exist and deduce they are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: show existence of A (or y), then 'suppose A' and A'' both satisfy the property; transform equalities to show A'=A''. Examples: uniqueness of inverse elements: assume y and y' with zy = z/x etc., plug a particular z (often 1) or manipulate algebraically to conclude equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving biconditionals by proving both directions separately
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements of the form P ⇔ Q, prove P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P as independent arguments, choosing the appropriate techniques for each direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints often say: 'prove both directions of the biconditional separately.' For the '⇒' direction choose direct or contradiction methods; for the '⇐' often construct explicit witnesses or solve an equation for the required variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve equations to find witnesses or inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the existential witness is defined by an equation, solve the equation algebraically to express the witness in terms of other variables; then verify the solution and optionally prove uniqueness by reversing steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: solving x + y = xy for y, solving for y in inverse-function constructions, or deriving formulas such as g(x) = (3x−5)/2 to be the inverse of f. Check domain restrictions and uniqueness by substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard induction structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mathematical induction by clearly stating the base case, assuming the inductive hypothesis for n, and proving the statement for n+1 (or using strong induction where appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sums formula, polynomial/divisibility proofs. Show base-case verification, then algebraic manipulation in the induction step. When using inequalities, carefully justify monotonicity/estimates in the step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove absolute values by case splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: To handle absolute-value inequalities, split into sign cases for the inner expression to convert absolute values into linear inequalities, then proceed algebraically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Prove |2x−6| > x when |x−4|>2 by considering x−4>0 and x−4<0 separately to determine sign and rewrite |·|. Mirror for reverse direction. Explicitly note which expression is positive/negative in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To refute a purported theorem, provide an explicit concrete example (values or sets) that violates the claimed statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many counterexamples are given: e.g., show a theorem is incorrect by choosing small finite sets A, B, C. Provide a clear check that the counterexample satisfies the hypotheses but not the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definitions precisely when working with relations and closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the formal definitions of reflexive/symmetric/transitive closures, minimality, and related concepts; typically prove closure properties by subset relations and use minimality/uniqueness arguments via inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prove R' (restriction) reflexive/transitive/antisymmetric by showing R' = R ∩ (A'×A') and using properties of R; show symmetric/transitive closures are smallest relations with those properties by set-inclusion arguments. When proving 'smallest' or 'minimal', show any other candidate contains yours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulating families of sets (unions/intersections of families)
rubrics_metrics.description: When sets are indexed families, choose an element from the member family and use membership rules for unions and intersections to prove inclusions and disjointness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns: to show x ∈ U(F∪G) pick A ∈ F∪G with x∈A and split cases; when proving pairwise disjointness of F∪G show elements from different subfamilies are disjoint. Beware of incorrectly asserting existence of a set that is simultaneously in two distinct families unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure nonemptiness when choosing an element from a set-of-sets
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof requires picking an element from a set Y ∈ B, ensure Y is nonempty (exclude empty set from the family if necessary) so existential instantiation is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in a proof involving relation S defined on a family B, the empty set must be excluded so you can choose y ∈ Y. The text explicitly notes necessity: 'The empty set had to be excluded from B so that we could come up with y ∈ Y in this proof.' If the empty set is allowed, include a counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove function properties by element-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is injective, assume f(x)=f(x') and deduce x=x' (often via algebra). To show surjective, for arbitrary b∈B, construct or find an a∈A with f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: algebraic proof that a given formula is one-to-one by manipulation; show onto by solving for preimage. For restrictions f|C, use (f|C)(c)=f(c) and appropriate domain/range arguments. For inverses, construct g and check f∘g= id and g∘f= id.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vacuous/invalid uses of statements (check hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful when applying implications or universal statements whose antecedents may be false; recognize when a statement is vacuously true and ensure you haven't inadvertently used that as a proof of an intended non-vacuous claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example remark: an asymmetric relation statement is vacuously true when xRy ∧ yRx is always false. Also check domain restrictions (e.g., denominators nonzero) when dividing or manipulating algebraic expressions.
